summary:
ASTROVYNEX is an intelligent, offline-first clinical decision support engine to protect crew health on long duration deep space transit. Crews travelling to Mars are exposed to extreme spaceflight hazards of ionising radiation, extreme isolation, and microgravity fluid shifts, plus a 20 minute one-way communication latency with Earth. Ground flight surgeons cannot provide real-time assistance and complete crew medical autonomy is a requirement.

To address this challenge, we built an on-device software suite with a Rosetta Universal Ingestion Layer to bridge aerospace hardware fragmentation.It successfully combines disparate, multi-vehicle telemetry streams – including blood oxygen (SpO₂), heart rate, white blood cell counts, and habitat radiation levels – into a centralised timeline interface. 

Instead of generic population red-lines that alert too late, ASTROVYNEX uses a personalised AI engine. The backend establishes a rolling 7-day baseline unique to each astronaut’s historical norm and uses statistical modelling to detect subtle, multi-system directional drift days before clinical symptoms appear. 

This innovation is critical as it shifts deep-space medicine from reactive crisis containment on Earth to predictive autonomous mitigation within the spacecraft, affording full healthcare independence when earh is just a blue dot
details:
How It Works and What It Does
ASTROVYNEX is an offline-first, free-standing clinical decision support engine that runs on the crew hardware to provide astronaut health monitoring without needing Earth connectivity.
1. Ingestion Layer (The Rosetta Bridge) It is a universal parser that normalizes disparate telemetry streams such as wearable smart shirt metrics (heart rate, HRV, SpO2, skin temperature), life-support spacesuit telemetry, and daily radiation dosimeter files into one common database.
2. The AI Drift Engine. It calculates a rolling 7-day personalized physiological baseline (mean and standard deviation) for each crew member. Statistical z-scores and multi-day directional trend vectors are used to assess new readings. If three parameters move down together over 4 days (e.g., HRV falling, fatigue, and resting heart rate rising), the system flags a “Watch” or “Escalate” alert before hard population safety limits are breached.
3. Interactive Visual Interface: Statistical drifts are displayed on a clickable, color-coded human silhouette. Select a body area and you’ll get an explainable diagnostic drawer with information about the spaceflight hazard, step-by-step guides to self-exams, and actionable countermeasure protocols.

Project’s Impact and Benefits
Full Healthcare Independence: Eliminates dependency on real-time Earth support, completely avoiding the 40-minute round trip radio delay during Mars transit.
Elimination of False Alarms: Removes false positives due to natural human variation by using personalized analytics rather than generic static population thresholds.
Hardware Agnostic: Translates metrics easily as astronauts shift from launch capsules to habitats and spacesuits, overcoming vehicle and sensor fragmentation.
High Terrestrial Scalability ("The Earth Twin"): Its low-compute, offline-first design has huge dual-use implications for Earth’s isolated environments, from polar research bases and maritime shipping fleets to remote mining teams and rural telehealth clinics with spotty internet.
Tools, Languages, Hardware & Software Used in Development: Python, JS/TS for core data pipeline and UI orchestration.
Backend Data Framework: Locally used Pandas and NumPy to build the rolling baseline calibration models and calculate rolling z-score time-series drifts.
 Database & UI Interface: SQLite/IndexedDB for encrypted offline persistence of data locally, along with standard HTML5/CSS3 and React for interactive human body silhouette and chart components.
Public Data Calibration: Built with data schemas and ranges sourced from the NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), Ames Life Sciences Data Archive (ALSDA), and historical solar storm JSON data from the NASA CCMC DONKI web Portal.


Creative Innovation & Factors That Are Considered
ASTROVITAL is a very creative project, because it takes medical tracking from passive, table-heavy data spreadsheets to immersive, context-aware anatomical dashboards.
Our team specifically took into account the following critical spaceflight factors:
Cognitive Overload: Stressed astronauts aren't able to interpret raw spreadsheets. We have built a simple and intuitive visual interface that does not require any medical expertise.
Zero-Burden Workflows: The system automatically cleans zero-gravity movement artifacts by cross-referencing metrics like skin temperature and respiration to avoid sensor-shifting false alarms.
Bandwidth Constrained Sync Queue—Store compressed computable clinical summaries offline until a communications link is established with the Earth before sending other transmittals.
